title: H-1B FY2027 Cap Filled With No Second Lottery as Wage-Weighted Selection Reshapes Visa Race
excerpt: The first cap season under the new wage-based lottery saw registrations plunge 38.5 percent, selection rates surge past 50 percent, and a decisive tilt toward higher-paid workers — fundamentally altering the calculus for Indian professionals and their employers.
body:
• USCIS confirmed the FY2027 H-1B cap is filled at 85,000 visas with no second lottery planned, after registrations fell 38.5% to 211,600 — the sharpest decline in years.
  • The first-ever wage-weighted selection system gave senior roles up to four times the selection odds of entry-level positions, with 71.5% of selected beneficiaries holding US advanced degrees.
  • Immigration law firm Fragomen reported selection rates above 50% for some employers, up from 35% in FY2026, as the $100,000 offshore hiring fee and $215 registration fee discouraged speculative filings.
  • Approved H-1B workers under the FY2027 cap can begin employment from October 1, 2026, as USCIS processes petitions filed during the April–June window.

The United States has closed the book on the FY2027 H-1B visa cap season — and the numbers tell the story of a program undergoing its most significant structural overhaul in nearly two decades.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services confirmed on March 31 that it had received enough electronic registrations to fill all 85,000 H-1B cap slots, including the 20,000 reserved for holders of US advanced degrees. With the June 30 petition filing deadline now passed, USCIS has confirmed there will be no second lottery for this fiscal year, according to Outlook Business.

Registrations Plunge, Selection Rates Soar

The FY2027 season saw 211,600 valid registrations — a 38.5% drop from the 343,981 received for FY2026, and a world away from the record 780,000-plus registrations that overwhelmed the system just a few years ago, according to USCIS data.

The decline was driven by a convergence of policy changes. USCIS raised the per-registration fee from $10 to $215, forcing employers to register only candidates they were committed to hiring. The agency also tied selections to unique beneficiaries' passports, eliminating the incentive for multiple employers to submit duplicate registrations for the same worker.

The result: a dramatically less crowded field. Immigration law firm Fragomen reported average selection rates above 50%, with some employers seeing rates as high as 65%. That compares with just 35% in FY2026 and 26% in FY2024.

How the Wage-Weighted Lottery Works

FY2027 marked the first cap season under a weighted selection process finalised by the Department of Homeland Security on December 29, 2025. Instead of equal odds in a random draw, the new system assigns lottery entries based on Department of Labor wage levels:

Positions at Level IV (senior roles) receive four entries in the selection pool, Level III receives three, Level II receives two, and Level I (entry-level) receives just one. DHS estimated a Level IV position would carry roughly a 61% chance of selection, compared with approximately 15% for Level I.

The data bears this out. USCIS reported that 71.5% of selected beneficiaries held a US advanced degree — up from 57% in FY2026. Only 17.7% of selected registrations came from the lowest wage category.

"Although selection is welcome news, it does not confer H-1B status; it merely authorizes the employer to file an H-1B petition during the filing window."

— Michael Castiglione, Attorney, Akerman LLP

The $100,000 Fee Factor

Compounding the shift, a September 2025 presidential proclamation imposed a $100,000 surcharge on H-1B petitions filed for beneficiaries located outside the United States. The fee does not apply to change-of-status filings for workers already in the country — a critical distinction for Indian professionals on F-1 student visas using Optional Practical Training.

"High-volume foreign recruitment is no longer financially viable for most companies since a single offshore hire now requires a six-figure investment before onboarding begins," immigration attorneys at Adams and Reese wrote in their analysis. The firm noted the fee is pushing employers to prioritise US-educated international graduates already in the country.

What It Means for Indian Professionals

The changes strike at the heart of the Indian H-1B pipeline. An estimated 1.43 lakh Indian nationals were on OPT or STEM OPT during the FY2027 registration window. For those in entry-level roles — typically classified at OEWS Level I — the new system slashed selection odds from roughly 30% under the old random lottery to just 15%.

Indian IT services companies that historically filed large volumes of H-1B petitions for workers based in India now face prohibitive costs, while employers hiring from US university campuses — where Indians form the largest cohort of international students — are exempt from the $100,000 fee. Immigration practitioners say the combined effect is a structural pivot favouring experienced professionals already within the US immigration system over fresh hires from abroad.

What Comes Next

USCIS is adjudicating petitions filed during the April–June window, with approved FY2027 H-1B workers eligible to begin employment from October 1, 2026. The agency has warned of heightened scrutiny — petitions must precisely match the wage level and beneficiary details submitted during registration.

For FY2028, immigration attorneys recommend companies begin wage-level assessments months earlier and budget for the higher compensation the weighted system rewards.
image_caption: An H-1B visa stamp in a passport, the specialty-occupation work permit that allows US employers to hire skilled foreign professionals. USCIS confirmed the FY2027 H-1B numerical cap has been reached, with no second lottery planned.
nri_angle: The new wage-weighted lottery disadvantages entry-level Indian professionals — an estimated 1.43 lakh OPT holders — while the $100,000 offshore fee incentivises employers to hire from the domestic F-1 pipeline instead of sponsoring workers directly from India.
author: Diaspora Desk
